question: Which motion degrees of freedom of levitated nanospheres have been experimentally studied?

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: Answer explicitly names the motion degrees of freedom experimentally studied: translation (center-of-mass), torsion/libration, rotation, precession, and nutation of levitated nanoparticles.
examples: Studied DOF include COM translation, libration, rotation, precession and nutation
Both translational and multiple rotational DOF have been explored experimentally

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: Answer states that Brownian motion of levitated microspheres/nanospheres was studied via the translational degrees of freedom, including direct measurement of the instantaneous velocity, verification of energy equipartition, and observation of the ballistic regime and ballistic-to-diffusive crossover.
examples: The instantaneous velocity of an optically trapped Brownian particle in air/vacuum was measured, verifying equipartition
The ballistic regime of Brownian motion was observed at short times

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: Answer states that translational motion was cooled, e.g., via feedback cooling with forces proportional to instantaneous velocity applied along orthogonal axes, reaching millikelvin temperatures for trapped microspheres.
examples: Three orthogonal cooling beams applied counter-velocity feedback forces
Millikelvin cooling of an optically trapped microsphere was achieved

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: Answer states that translational motion was used for ultrasensitive force (and acceleration) detection, citing yoctonewton-level resolution (~166 yN) and zN/Hz^1/2-scale sensitivity characterized via Allan variance analysis.
examples: Force resolution of ~166 yN at optimal measurement time, with ~6.3 zN/Hz^1/2 sensitivity
Applications include fifth-force searches and gravitational-wave detection

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies librational (torsional) oscillation of ellipsoidal nanoparticles' long axis about its equilibrium alignment with the polarization of a linearly polarized Gaussian trapping beam, detected via polarization changes of the light.
examples: The long axis of an ellipsoidal nanoparticle oscillates about the light polarization direction
Librational oscillations are read out from polarization changes of the laser

ingredients.name: answer_critical_5
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies rotation of dumbbell-shaped nanoparticles driven by circularly polarized light, reaching frequencies above 1 GHz and measured through polarization modulation of the transmitted light.
examples: A levitated dumbbell nanoparticle rotates at over 1 GHz under circular polarization
The rotation frequency is inferred from polarization modulation of the beam

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: Answer notes that rotational degrees of freedom enable precision torque measurement, citing sensitivities around (4.2 ± 1.2) × 10^-27 Nm/Hz^1/2, among the most sensitive reported.
examples: GHz-rotating dumbbells serve as ultrasensitive torque detectors at the 10^-27 Nm/Hz^1/2 level
Torque detection with ~4.2 × 10^-27 Nm/Hz^1/2 sensitivity was achieved

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: Answer mentions that precession and nutation of non-spherical nanoparticles were experimentally observed in agreement with theoretical predictions, with potential torque precision of (3.6 ± 1.1) × 10^-31 Nm/Hz^1/2 at pressures below 10^-7 mbar.
examples: Precession and nutation were observed in high vacuum, matching theory
At <10^-7 mbar, torque precision could in principle reach ~3.6 × 10^-31 Nm/Hz^1/2
